COLORS LESSON · COLORS & SHADES · AGES 2–5 YEARS

Black — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches the color black: penguin suits, piano keys, the boldest color in the box.

What is this?

Black is a color — the color of the penguin, the piano, the black cat and the tire on the card. It is the darkest color there is, and it makes every other color next to it shine.

What does it mean?

Black is the bold color: tuxedos, pianos, night sky. Your child is learning the color that artists use to draw the OUTLINE — the color of edges and shapes.

What does the child need to know?

The child needs to: say "black", meet black on two animals (penguin, cat), one instrument (piano) and one thing with wheels (tire), and notice black-and-white pairs.

Why this matters

Black-and-white noticing is a real milestone — newborns see it first, and this card (with its white-bellied penguin and white-keyed piano) is full of the pair.

What it teaches

Vocabulary, contrast awareness (black on white pops), animal movement vocabulary (waddle), and a first instrument meet — the piano keys are a keyboard waiting to be touched.

Words to learn

blackpenguinpianocattirewaddlekeysnightshinesuit

Say this to your child

“"Black! The penguin is black, the piano is black, the cat is black, the tire is black. Black is the boldest color. Waddle like a penguin! Tinkle like a piano! Now sneak… like the black cat."”

Step by step

  1. Point and name: penguin — black, piano — black, cat — black, tire — black. Two animals, one instrument, one wheel.
  2. The suit story: the penguin’s back is black and its tummy is white — swimming below, hunters looking UP see white sky; hunters above see black sea. The suit is a disguise. Mind blown, gently.
  3. The keys game: the piano has black keys AND white keys — count three black keys on the card with one finger, plink plink plink, voice as piano.
  4. Waddle race: feet together, arms at sides, waddle the hallway saying "black, black, black". Penguins never run; the race is won by the best waddle.
  5. Close with the cat: quiet, sneaky, soft steps — the black cat lap back. Cats nap; so does the lesson. Good night, black.

Look closer at the picture

Every square hides a white part — the penguin’s tummy, the piano’s keys, the cat’s (missing here, but the tire’s tread pattern shows the road). Black never travels alone; it brings its contrast.

Ask your child

"Which black animal cannot fly but swims like a torpedo?" (penguin) "Which black thing has keys but no doors?" (piano) "What rolls and goes vroom?" (tire)

What your child can say or do

Your child might waddle on every errand for a week or plink out songs on the kitchen counter. The piano square’s fans are easy to spot — they are the ones drumming.

Out in the real world

Penguins live south — the Antarctic and up to South Africa and New Zealand; zoos bring the waddle to town. Pianos have 88 keys, 36 of them black — the number comes later, the plinking starts now.

Try it together

Black-key song: draw a paper keyboard, five white keys and three black keys, and "play" it while humming — every black key press must be announced: "BLACK!" Composing and color naming in one sitting.

Understanding check

Ask: "what color is the piano?" (black) "Waddle like the penguin." (the waddle confirms) "What is the opposite of black? Try white!" (the pair, named)

This lesson pairs with the Black flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Colors & Shades.
